chapter: Guitarists and the Pierron and Brown bands
title: Thompson McKay and Snoozer Quinn, the greatest guitarist
summary: Thompson McKay played plantation-style guitar. Snoozer Quinn is called the best guitarist ever, with vibrato, a violin stunt, and a stint with the Owls at Suburban Gardens.

story.theme_name: Banjo, guitar and the rhythm section: instruments and players
story.community_name: Banjo, guitar and the rhythm section's changing role

blocks.x: And it just messed me up. I couldn't get that stroke. Now, Thompson McKay, there were two brothers, Percy and Thompson. Percy is one of the vice presidents of the Whitney Bank. Thompson's a consulting engineer in Dallas for one of the very big engineering firms. He was better than Percy and he had that Negro style down pat. He played just exactly like they did in the cornfield plantation stuff. Now, the best guitarist that I ever heard any place, and I don't think there'll ever be one before or after, no matter how much that technique is brilliant for single string stuff, Snooze of Quinn will never be ever touched by anybody. Now, he played with an unamplified guitar except for the last five years of his life. And that was the most discreet amplification I've ever heard. You couldn't tell it was amplified at all, except that everybody in the room could hear it. And he had a vibrato that he used with his foot on this thing that was terrific, too. Yeah. That was a sustained note. But he'd have the whole thing, the lead, the treble, the lead, the accompaniment, and the bass going at one time.
You can hear that on those records that Johnny had him to record. Yes, indeed. Did he do much better than that? Those are plenty good.
Well, yes, he did much better than that.
Of course, he was sick in the hospital and all that. I wondered if he did.
Now, another thing, too, that not much is mentioned about Snooze that could sing to beat hell. And he was a marvelous violin player. Did you know that, too, Johnny?
Somebody told me that once, but I never did.

He did this old stunt that Joe Venuti does. He loosened the bow until the horsehair was very loose. And then he'd put it upside down over the thing. And he'd play four chord tunes on the thing, which was fabulous. But any place that Snooze would win, nobody would play there. Everybody would quit and just go around. Even up at the Tulane gym, if you brought it up there, all of them would quit and listen to him. But he didn't care to practice. He practiced maybe six or eight hours, but never formally. He'd practice alone for himself.
He didn't care. Did you ever play in any bands as much around here?
I know he did some, but I never heard of anything special. and things like that.
Things like that as well. No good bands.
Oh, the owls. He played with them for a while. I remember him playing out at Suburban Gardens with the owls.
